Internal Policy Document

Document ID: POL-5G-005
Title: 5G Coverage, Troubleshooting, and Device Compatibility FAQ
Version: 1.9
Effective date: 2026-04-01
Owner: Network Product
Classification: Internal. Answers in this FAQ may be paraphrased for customers.
Applies to: Prodapt 5G and 4G LTE handset service in the United States. Roaming behavior is in the roaming policy. Bill credits are in the billing and SLA policies.

1. Purpose

This FAQ answers how Prodapt 5G works, why it is often slower indoors, which phones are compatible, and the handset checks support should try before blaming a tower.

This FAQ does not contain live tower status, packet loss, open incidents, or outage history. Those come from the network database. If the customer names a tower id or a city and says service is dropping right now, the network diagnostic has to be run. Do not answer that question from this FAQ alone.

2. What 5G means on Prodapt

Prodapt uses three 5G layers:

- Low-band 5G. Wide coverage, indoor reach similar to LTE, speeds often close to strong LTE. Used to keep a 5G icon in suburban and rural areas.
- Mid-band 5G on bands n41 and n77. This is the capacity layer in cities. It is the layer customers mean when they expect a clear speed increase over LTE.
- Millimeter wave (mmWave) on bands n260 and n261. Very high speed, very short range, poor building penetration. Used in dense downtown pockets such as transit hubs and stadiums. A phone must specifically support mmWave. Most phones that "have 5G" do not.

The phone decides the layer. The customer cannot force mid-band from the bill plan. Unlimited Plus, Unlimited Essential, Business Unlimited, and Enterprise Mobile all include 5G where the phone and the site support it. There is no extra 5G access fee.

3. Why 5G is slow or drops indoors

Building materials attenuate radio signals. Concrete, low-emissivity glass, and metal reduce mid-band. They block millimeter wave almost completely.

Typical indoor loss is 10 to 20 dB on mid-band and far more on millimeter wave. A phone that shows an acceptable outdoor signal can be marginal or poor once the customer walks inside. As a rule of thumb, an outdoor reading near -70 dBm can land near -90 to -100 dBm indoors, and a millimeter-wave session will usually fall back to mid-band or LTE.

Slow indoor 5G is usually one of these:

- The phone was on millimeter wave outside and fell back indoors. Speeds drop sharply. This is expected.
- The phone is on mid-band but the indoor signal is marginal. Throughput falls and sessions may drop while the signal indicator still shows a few bars, because bars are not a packet-loss reading.
- The site itself is congested or impaired. A strong signal with dropping sessions is a site problem, not an indoor-coverage problem. That case is decided by tower status, packet loss, and throughput, which are not in this FAQ.
- Wi-Fi is connected but the Wi-Fi path is failing, and the customer believes it is cellular. Ask whether the drop happens with Wi-Fi turned off.

What to tell the customer about indoor slowness:

1. Step near a window or step outside and retest. If it recovers, the building is the attenuator.
2. Turn on Wi-Fi calling for voice if the customer has reliable Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi calling is included on all Prodapt plans at no charge.
3. Confirm the phone supports n41 and n77 (section 5). A phone with low-band only will feel like LTE inside buildings.
4. If the problem continues outdoors, or the customer can name a tower or a street corner where it drops with a strong signal, stop the handset checklist and run a network diagnostic. Do not keep resetting a phone when the site is the suspect.

4. Dropped 5G sessions when the signal looks fine

Bars and a single signal reading do not prove the site is healthy. Sessions drop when packet loss is elevated or when downlink throughput collapses, including on a site whose status is still operational and whose signal is still acceptable (around -70 dBm).

Handset steps, in order, and only when a site diagnostic has not already shown loss or an open incident:

1. Toggle airplane mode for 15 seconds.
2. Confirm the phone is not in LTE-only mode.
3.

3. Confirm the phone supports n41 and n77 (section 5). A phone with low-band only will feel like LTE inside buildings.
4. If the problem continues outdoors, or the customer can name a tower or a street corner where it drops with a strong signal, stop the handset checklist and run a network diagnostic. Do not keep resetting a phone when the site is the suspect.

4. Dropped 5G sessions when the signal looks fine

Bars and a single signal reading do not prove the site is healthy. Sessions drop when packet loss is elevated or when downlink throughput collapses, including on a site whose status is still operational and whose signal is still acceptable (around -70 dBm).

Handset steps, in order, and only when a site diagnostic has not already shown loss or an open incident:

1. Toggle airplane mode for 15 seconds.
2. Confirm the phone is not in LTE-only mode.
3. Install the current carrier settings and operating system update.
4. Remove and reseat the SIM, or re-download the eSIM profile if the line uses eSIM.
5. Test with Wi-Fi off, standing still, for one minute.
6. If a second Prodapt phone at the same spot drops the same way, it is not the first handset. Run the site diagnostic.

Factory reset is not the first step and is not the fix for a site impairment.

5. Device compatibility

A phone is compatible with Prodapt 5G mid-band when it supports bands n41 and n77 and is on the list below. Low-band only phones may show a 5G icon and still feel like LTE.

Supported for Prodapt mid-band 5G (n41 and n77):
- Apple iPhone 12 and newer, including iPhone 13, iPhone 13 mini, iPhone 13 Pro, and iPhone 13 Pro Max
- Apple iPhone SE (3rd generation, 2022) and newer
- Samsung Galaxy S21 and newer, Galaxy A54 and newer
- Google Pixel 6 and newer

Millimeter wave on Prodapt, in addition to mid-band, requires a US mmWave model:
- iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16 US models (not the mini models, which do not include mmWave)
- Samsung Galaxy S21, S22, S23, and S24 Ultra US models
- Pixel 6 Pro, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 8 Pro, and Pixel 9 Pro US models

Not compatible with Prodapt 5G:
- iPhone 11 and older. These are LTE only. They still work on the Prodapt 4G LTE network. An upgrade is optional, not required for voice and basic data. Trade-in values are in the device upgrade policy.
- Unlocked phones that lack n41 and n77, even if they show a 5G logo for another carrier's bands.

An iPhone 13 is compatible with Prodapt 5G mid-band. It is not the cause of a site-wide drop by itself. Whether the customer may trade that iPhone 13 in is answered by the device upgrade policy, not by this FAQ.

6. Coverage expectations

Prodapt sells 5G coverage as outdoor coverage at the address level. Indoor coverage is not guaranteed, especially for millimeter wave and especially in basements and interior rooms.
A coverage map gap outdoors, confirmed by a diagnostic with poor signal (weaker than -110 dBm) and a healthy site, is a coverage limitation. Offer Wi-Fi calling. Do not invent a truck roll from this FAQ.
5G Home is a fixed indoor receiver with its own install rules. It is not a handset plan and does not use this handset checklist.

7. When to stop using this FAQ

Stop and use the network diagnostic when the customer:

- Names a tower id (the id looks like a state abbreviation, a hyphen, and a number)
- Says service drops in one neighborhood but not others
- Reports an outage, a dead site, or many people affected
- Has already completed the handset steps in section 4

Stop and use the SLA policy when the customer asks whether an outage earns a credit.
Stop and use the roaming policy when the customer is outside the United States.

8. Symptom guide

No bars, or the phone says SOS or emergency calls only.
The phone is not registered on Prodapt or any roaming partner. Have the customer toggle airplane mode, confirm the SIM is seated, and confirm the line is not suspended. If a second Prodapt phone in the same spot also shows SOS, stop handset steps and run a tower diagnostic. One phone on SOS and another working is the handset or the SIM.

Stop and use the roaming policy when the customer is outside the United States.

8. Symptom guide

No bars, or the phone says SOS or emergency calls only.
The phone is not registered on Prodapt or any roaming partner. Have the customer toggle airplane mode, confirm the SIM is seated, and confirm the line is not suspended. If a second Prodapt phone in the same spot also shows SOS, stop handset steps and run a tower diagnostic. One phone on SOS and another working is the handset or the SIM.

5G icon is on, speed test is slow, only indoors.
Section 3. Window test. Wi-Fi calling for voice. This is the usual indoor mid-band or millimeter-wave case. If the slow speed continues outdoors at the same corner, run a tower diagnostic.

5G icon is on, signal looks strong, sessions still drop.
Bars are not packet loss. A strong reading can sit next to elevated loss or collapsed downlink. Run a tower diagnostic when the customer can name a place or a tower. Do not factory-reset first.

Works on Wi-Fi, fails on cellular.
Turn Wi-Fi off and retest. If cellular then fails in one neighborhood only, run a tower diagnostic. If cellular fails everywhere and Wi-Fi works, check suspension, SIM, and whether the line is active before blaming a tower.

Hotspot or tethering is slow while the phone itself is fine.
Hotspot uses the same plan. Unlimited Plus, Unlimited Essential, Business Unlimited, and Enterprise Mobile include hotspot. After a heavy hotspot day the phone may be deprioritized behind other traffic on a busy site. Deprioritization is not an outage and is not an SLA credit. It clears as the site gets quieter. 5G Home is not a hotspot line.

Dual SIM, and Prodapt is the second line.
The phone may prefer the other SIM for data. Set the Prodapt line as the data line and retest. This is a handset setting, not a tower fault.

eSIM will not download.
The line must be ACTIVE, not suspended or cancelled. The phone must be on Wi-Fi or on a working cellular connection from the other SIM. A failed eSIM download is not a coverage gap.

Voicemail or calls fail, data works.
Confirm VoLTE is on. Prodapt voice on 5G and LTE uses VoLTE. A phone forced to 2G or with VoLTE off will drop calls on a healthy data site. Turn VoLTE on before opening a tower ticket.

5G at home is a fixed gateway, not a phone.
5G Home uses a gateway at the service address. It does not roam. It does not use the handset checklist. A gateway offline at the address is a site or install issue, not an iPhone issue.

9. Settings that are safe to quote

Prodapt does not require a custom APN on current iPhone and major Android models. If an unlocked phone asks for an APN, use the APN name prodapt, the APN prodapt, and leave username and password empty.
Wi-Fi calling is included at no charge on every plan.
There is no paid "5G booster" add-on. Anyone selling one is not Prodapt.
Low-band keeps a 5G icon in suburban and rural areas. Mid-band (n41 and n77) is the city capacity layer. Millimeter wave is downtown pockets only and falls off indoors.

10. More compatibility notes

iPhone 13, 13 mini, 13 Pro, and 13 Pro Max support Prodapt mid-band 5G.
iPhone 13 mini does not support millimeter wave. iPhone 13, 13 Pro, and 13 Pro Max US models do.
iPhone 11 and older are LTE only. They still place calls and use data on the 4G LTE network. An upgrade is optional.
A phone bought for another carrier must be unlocked and must support n41 and n77 before it is treated as 5G-capable on Prodapt.
Watches paired to a supported iPhone use the phone's cellular plan. A watch with its own number is a second line and needs its own SIM or eSIM. Trade-in values for phones are in the device upgrade policy. This FAQ does not set trade-in prices.

11. Worked questions

Why is my 5G slow indoors?
Buildings cut mid-band by about 10 to 20 dB and block millimeter wave. Step to a window, turn on Wi-Fi calling, and confirm the phone supports n41 and n77. If it is also slow outdoors, run a tower diagnostic.

Can I use an iPhone 13 on Prodapt 5G?
Yes for mid-band.

They still place calls and use data on the 4G LTE network. An upgrade is optional.
A phone bought for another carrier must be unlocked and must support n41 and n77 before it is treated as 5G-capable on Prodapt.
Watches paired to a supported iPhone use the phone's cellular plan. A watch with its own number is a second line and needs its own SIM or eSIM. Trade-in values for phones are in the device upgrade policy. This FAQ does not set trade-in prices.

11. Worked questions

Why is my 5G slow indoors?
Buildings cut mid-band by about 10 to 20 dB and block millimeter wave. Step to a window, turn on Wi-Fi calling, and confirm the phone supports n41 and n77. If it is also slow outdoors, run a tower diagnostic.

Can I use an iPhone 13 on Prodapt 5G?
Yes for mid-band. That does not say whether the customer may trade it in, and it does not say a particular tower is healthy.

The whole neighborhood is down.
This FAQ cannot confirm an outage. Use the outage log and the tower diagnostic. Credits, if any, come from the SLA policy after the duration and account type are known.

I am traveling outside the United States and 5G is slow.
Use the roaming policy. This FAQ is for the Prodapt network inside the United States. Japan and Western Europe prices are not answered here.

12. Document control

Indoor loss of 10 to 20 dB on mid-band, Wi-Fi calling at no charge, and the iPhone 12-and-newer compatibility rule including iPhone 13 are unchanged in version 1.9. Live site health remains outside this document.

Document ID: POL-BILL-003
Title: Billing Disputes, Duplicate Charges, and Credit Approval
Version: 5.0
Effective date: 2026-02-01
Owner: Billing Resolution
Classification: Internal. Required for any credit posted to a Prodapt account.
Applies to: All consumer, business, and enterprise bills.

1. Purpose

This policy controls how long a customer has to dispute a charge, which charges may be credited, and when a credit may be applied immediately versus when it must wait for a supervisor.

Account balances, charge lines, and duplicate flags are not stored in this document. They are in the billing database. An agent must look up the account before quoting a balance or stating that a duplicate exists.

2. Dispute window

A customer has 60 days from the charge date to open a dispute.
The charge date is the date on the charge line, not the date the customer noticed it.
A dispute opened on day 60 is still in time. A dispute opened on day 61 is late and must be declined unless a billing supervisor grants a one-time exception, which is recorded on the dispute.
The window applies to plan charges, add-ons, roaming, device installments, taxes billed in error, and late fees.

How to answer "how long do I have to dispute a charge?":
You have 60 days from the charge date.

3. What may be credited

- A duplicate charge: the same description and the same billing period posted more than once, or a charge line with the duplicate flag set.
- A roaming charge that violates the roaming policy (for example Travel Pass plus pay-per-use for the same data). Ordinary published roaming rates are not credits.
- An SLA credit that the SLA policy says is owed.
- A device installment or add-on the customer did not authorize, when the order system has no matching order.
- A tax billed on a tax-exempt enterprise account, with the exemption certificate already on file.

4. What must not be credited

- Usage the customer actually incurred at a published rate.
- A charge older than 60 days, unless a supervisor exception is on the dispute.
- A second credit for the same charge id.
- Cash, check, or external refund. Credits reduce the Prodapt account balance or sit pending. They are not sent as a payment to the customer.
- An amount that is still only a guess. Look up the charge before choosing the credit amount.

5. How to identify a duplicate

Treat a charge as a duplicate when either of these is true:

a. The charge line's duplicate flag is set, or
b. Another charge for the same customer has the same description and the same billing period.

The credit amount for a duplicate is the amount of the extra line, once. If two identical plan charges posted, credit one of them, not both. Leave one valid charge on the account.
If the flag is set and the description also matches another line in that period, that is one duplicate, not two.

6. Auto-approval limit

The auto-approval limit is 50.00 USD per credit.

- If the credit amount is 50.00 USD or less, the credit is auto-approved.
  Record the credit with status APPLIED.
  Reduce the account's current balance by the credit amount.
  The new balance must not go below zero. If it would, apply only enough to bring the balance to zero and leave a note. Do not create a cash refund for the remainder.

- If the credit amount is greater than 50.00 USD, the credit is not auto-approved.
  Record the credit with status PENDING_APPROVAL.
  Do not change the current balance.
  The balance changes only after a billing supervisor approves the row and the status becomes APPLIED.
  Tell the customer the credit is submitted and waiting for approval. Do not say the credit has already been applied.

A supervisor may reject a pending credit. Set the status to REJECTED and leave the balance unchanged.

Credits above 200.00 USD follow the same PENDING_APPROVAL rule and also require a manager, not only a billing supervisor. The agent still must not reduce the balance at the time of the request.

Worked examples:

Example A. A duplicate monthly plan charge of 65.99 USD.
65.99 is greater than 50.00. Insert the credit as PENDING_APPROVAL. Do not reduce the balance. One valid plan charge remains.

Example B. A duplicate add-on of 12.00 USD.
12.00 is less than or equal to 50.00. Insert the credit as APPLIED and reduce the current balance by 12.00.

Example C. A credit of exactly 50.00 USD.

7. One dispute per charge

Open at most one active dispute (status OPEN or ESCALATED) per charge id.
If a dispute is already OPEN, do not open a second one and do not post a second credit. Update the existing dispute.
When a credit moves to APPLIED, set the related dispute to RESOLVED and record the credit id in the resolution notes.
When a credit is REJECTED, set the dispute to RESOLVED and state why it was denied.

8. Escalation

Escalate to a billing supervisor, and set the dispute status to ESCALATED, when:

- The credit is greater than 50.00 USD.
- The customer asks for more than the duplicate amount.
- The dispute is outside the 60 day window and the customer is asking for an exception.
- The account is Enterprise.
- Fraud is suspected (the customer denies the line entirely, or charges appear from a country the customer could not have visited). Fraud cases go to the fraud desk, not to a standard credit.

9. Audit

Every credit must be a row in the billing credits table with a customer id, an amount, a reason, a status, and a timestamp.
Do not change a balance with a manual note only. If the balance changes, an APPLIED credit row must explain the change.
Do not keep a side list of credits outside the billing database.
The reason text should name the charge description and the billing period, for example "Duplicate Unlimited Plus charge for 2026-09".

10. What support should tell the customer

State whether a duplicate was found, the amount, and whether the credit is APPLIED or PENDING_APPROVAL.
If the status is PENDING_APPROVAL, give the customer the dispute id and say a supervisor must approve credits over 50.00 USD.
If no duplicate exists, say so, and do not create a credit to be helpful.
Quote document id POL-BILL-003 when asked which policy was used.

11. SLA credits posted by billing

When the SLA policy says a customer is eligible, billing posts that dollar amount under this policy.
The SLA policy chooses eligibility and the formula. This policy chooses APPLIED versus PENDING_APPROVAL.
A 22.50 USD Business SLA credit is APPLIED.
A 62.25 USD Enterprise SLA credit is PENDING_APPROVAL because it is over 50.00 USD.

12. Same description is not always a duplicate

A plan that bills every month will show the same description in 2026-07, 2026-08, and 2026-09. Those are three periods, not a duplicate.
A duplicate requires the same customer, the same description, and the same billing period, or a line whose duplicate flag is set.
Credit one extra line, not every line that shares the description.
If a duplicate was already credited and that credit is APPLIED, do not credit it again. A resolved dispute is the record.
A PAID invoice from a prior month is history. Do not subtract that history from the current balance a second time.

14. Charges that look wrong but are not duplicates

A single Travel Pass or pay-per-use line at a price published in the roaming policy is not a duplicate. Examples: 60.00 USD for five Japan Zone C days (5 times 12.00), or a single Brazil Zone D data line. Decline the dispute. Do not insert a credit.
A sales-tax line next to a plan charge is not a duplicate of the plan. Different description.
A late fee is not a duplicate of the plan. If the payment posted after the due date, the late fee stands and any requested credit is REJECTED.
Zone A pay-per-use data on an Unlimited Plus line is a real billing error, because Unlimited Plus includes Canada and Mexico. Credit that pay-per-use amount under section 6. If that credit is already APPLIED, stop.
5G Home cannot roam. A roaming line on a 5G Home account is a billing error. Credit it if it is still inside 60 days and has not already been credited.

15. Lookup rules

Read the account from the billing database before quoting a balance, a name, or a charge.
The current balance equals the open charges, minus credits that were APPLIED against those open charges. Paid charges from prior months are not added again.

A suspended account with a past-due balance over 25.00 USD also cannot start a device upgrade. That rule is in the device upgrade policy. It does not change the credit limit here.

Document ID: POL-DEV-006
Title: Device Upgrade, Early Upgrade, and Trade-In Policy
Version: 2.2
Effective date: 2026-05-01
Owner: Device Lifecycle
Classification: Internal. Trade-in quotes in section 4 may be given to customers as estimates.
Applies to: Prodapt handset installment plans. Does not apply to 5G Home gateways or bring-your-own-device lines with no installment.

1. Purpose

This policy states when a customer may upgrade a handset, how the 36 month installment works, what early upgrade requires, and the trade-in credit for common devices. The iPhone 13 answers are in section 4 and section 6.

Account past-due status and the live balance are not in this document. Check the billing account before promising that a specific customer is eligible. This document says what the rules are.

2. Standard installment

New devices are financed over 36 months.
The monthly device installment is separate from the service plan (Unlimited Plus, Unlimited Essential, Business Unlimited, or Enterprise Mobile).
There is no interest on a Prodapt installment while the account stays active.
If the customer cancels service, the remaining device balance is due on the final bill.
Trade-in credit, once the device is received and graded, is applied to the new installment agreement. It is not paid as cash. If the trade-in credit is larger than the remaining balance the customer owes on the old device, the extra reduces the new device's installment. It does not become a check.

3. When a customer may upgrade

A customer may start a new installment when all of the following are true:

a. The account is in good standing. The past-due balance is 25.00 USD or less. A past-due balance above 25.00 USD blocks the upgrade until it is paid. The current bill that is not yet due does not count as past due.

b. The line is ACTIVE. Suspended and closed lines cannot upgrade.

c. One of these device conditions is true:
   - The current device is paid off (36 of 36 installments, or bought outright), or
   - Early upgrade in section 5 is satisfied, or
   - The customer will pay the remaining device balance in full at checkout.

Consumer, Business, and Enterprise use the same device rules. Enterprise lines still need the account to be in good standing. A business administrator must approve an enterprise upgrade; the support agent must not start the installment without that approval on the account.

4. Trade-in credit estimates

Credits below assume the device powers on, is not on a financial blacklist, and is not activation-locked to another person. The estimate is not final until Prodapt receives the device and grades it. The customer has 14 days from the new device ship date to send the trade-in. If the device does not arrive, the estimated credit is reversed onto the bill.

Condition grades:

- Good: powers on, no cracks, no liquid damage, battery holds a charge through a normal day.
- Fair: powers on, light scratches, small hairline crack that does not affect touch, battery still usable.
- Damaged: cracked glass across the display, liquid damage, or swollen battery, but the device still powers on.
- A device that does not power on has a trade-in value of 0.00 USD. It does not qualify for early-upgrade waiver of the remaining balance.

5. Early upgrade

Title: Network Outage Classification and NOC Procedures
Version: 2.6
Effective date: 2026-01-15
Owner: Network Operations Center
Classification: Internal. Support may quote the severity definitions. Do not quote internal bridge numbers to customers.
Applies to: All Prodapt radio sites and regional core networks in the United States.

1. Purpose

This document defines how Prodapt classifies an outage, what each tower status means, how the NOC works an incident, and how to read a live diagnostic. It is the source for the question "what defines a CRITICAL outage?"

The outage log stores individual events (region, severity, duration, customers affected, root cause). This document stores the rules. Do not treat an example in this document as a live event.

2. Severity definitions

Classify an event at the highest severity whose rule matches.

CRITICAL. Declare CRITICAL when any one of these is true:

1. 5,000 or more customers lose voice or data service, or
2. A regional core, packet gateway, or metro fiber ring fails, or
3. Two or more towers in the same city are OFFLINE at the same time, or
4. Customer-facing voice and data are fully unavailable and restoration is expected to take more than 60 minutes.

A fiber cut that isolates a regional ring is CRITICAL even before the final customer count is known, because rule 2 is already met.
An event that affects 5,000 or more customers is CRITICAL even if it is restored in under 60 minutes, because rule 1 is already met.

MAJOR. Declare MAJOR when the event is not CRITICAL and any one of these is true:

- 500 to 4,999 customers are affected, or
- A single tower is OFFLINE for more than 30 minutes, or
- Service is impaired across a site (calls or data fail intermittently) for more than 30 minutes.

MINOR. Declare MINOR when all of these are true:

- Fewer than 500 customers are affected, and
- No tower is fully OFFLINE for more than 30 minutes, and
- The impact is degraded performance or a short interruption under 30 minutes.

Planned maintenance that was announced at least 48 hours in advance is not an unplanned outage. Log it as maintenance. If it overruns the announced window, classify only the overrun using the rules above.

3. Tower status values

OPERATIONAL
The site is in service. A site can be OPERATIONAL and still be unhealthy. Elevated packet loss or collapsed throughput with status OPERATIONAL means the site is up and degraded. Do not tell the customer the tower is down.

DEGRADED
The site is carrying traffic below its normal capacity. Customers may see slow data or dropped sessions. This is not a full outage by itself.

OFFLINE
The site is not carrying customer traffic. Packet loss at 100 percent and throughput at zero are consistent with OFFLINE. Troubleshoot the site, not the handset.

MAINTENANCE
The site is in a planned window. Check whether the window was announced at least 48 hours ahead before discussing SLA credits. Planned maintenance is excluded from automatic SLA credits.

4. Incident classifications

Use exactly one classification on an open incident:

POWER                  Commercial power or generator failure
BACKHAUL               Fiber, microwave, or transport between the site and the core
RADIO_ACCESS           Radio unit, antenna, sector, or scheduler on the tower
CORE                   Regional packet core, mobility controller, or gateway
SOFTWARE               Bad configuration or software fault
PLANNED_MAINTENANCE    Announced maintenance window

5. Performance interpretation guide

Use the latest performance sample for the tower, not the average of older samples. Compare it to these thresholds:

Signal strength (dBm)
- Acceptable: -90 dBm or stronger (for example -72 dBm is acceptable).
- Marginal: weaker than -90 dBm and down to -110 dBm.
- Poor coverage: weaker than -110 dBm.

Packet loss
- Normal: 1 percent or below.
- Elevated: above 2 percent.
- Severe: above 5 percent.
- Site down: 100 percent, which should match status OFFLINE.

Latency
- Normal on 5G: 40 ms or below.
- Elevated: above 50 ms.

Downlink throughput
- A 5G tower that is OPERATIONAL and delivering below 100 Mbps downlink is degraded, even when the signal reading is acceptable.
- 4G LTE sites normally deliver less downlink than 5G.

- Status OFFLINE, or packet loss 100 percent: the site is down. Recommend field dispatch against the open incident. Do not advise the customer to factory-reset the phone as the fix.

- Signal poor (weaker than -110 dBm) and the site otherwise healthy: this is a coverage or indoor problem. Recommend a window test, Wi-Fi calling, and the 5G FAQ. Do not open a CRITICAL incident for one indoor handset.
- Status MAINTENANCE with classification PLANNED_MAINTENANCE: tell the customer the window end time. Do not file an SLA credit for the announced window.

6. NOC procedure

Step 1. Detect. Alarm, customer pattern, or a diagnostic that shows OFFLINE or severe loss.
Step 2. Classify using section 2 and section 4. Write the severity and the classification on the incident.
Step 3. Open or attach an incident. One active incident per site per fault. Do not open a second incident for the same tower and the same fault.
Step 4. Start the MTTR clock at the outage start, not at the time the ticket was typed.
       CRITICAL restore target: 4 hours. Update customers every 30 minutes.
       MAJOR restore target: 8 hours. Update every 60 minutes.
       MINOR restore target: 24 hours. Update every 4 hours.
Step 5. Bridge. CRITICAL events require a live bridge with the region on call. MAJOR events bridge if restoration will exceed 2 hours.
Step 6. Restore service, then take one confirming performance sample.
Step 7. Close the incident only after the confirming sample is healthy (packet loss at or below 1 percent, status no longer OFFLINE or DEGRADED).
Step 8. Write the historical outage row: region, severity, start, end, duration in hours, customers affected, root cause, and status RESOLVED. The open incident queue is not the historical log. Resolved events must not remain on the open queue.
Step 9. Post-incident review is required for every CRITICAL event and for any event that missed its MTTR target. The review is internal and is not quoted to customers.

7. Customer communication rules for NOC findings

Support may share: tower status, city, whether an incident is open, the incident id, the customer impact (down, slow, or dropping), and the last update time.
Support may not share: bridge phone numbers, vendor names on a contract, or a guess about fiber routes.
If no open incident exists and the latest sample is healthy, say the site looks healthy and follow the 5G FAQ for handset steps.
If an open incident exists, do not describe the tower as healthy just because status is OPERATIONAL.

8. Regions

Prodapt operates five regions for both towers and outages: Midwest, Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, and West.
A regional summary counts towers by status inside one region. It is not the same report as a historical outage count. Outage history is classified by the severity rules in section 2 and stored in the outage log.

9. Use the latest sample

Tower performance is a time series. A site can look healthy for several days and then fail on the newest reading.
Diagnostics, packet-loss rankings, and "is the tower up right now" all use the newest recorded time for that tower.
Do not average the week. An average will hide a site that went offline on the latest sample, and it will hide a site whose loss climbed only in the last day.
If the newest sample is healthy and an older sample was bad, say the site has recovered and quote the newest numbers.

10. How to read a diagnostic

Answer in this order: tower status, technology, city and region, newest signal, newest packet loss, newest latency, newest downlink, and any open incident id.

Pattern: status OPERATIONAL, 5G, signal acceptable (stronger than -90 dBm), packet loss above 2 percent, downlink below 100 Mbps.
The site is up. The phone is not the first suspect. Loss is elevated and throughput is degraded. Look for an open radio or backhaul incident. Tell the customer sessions can drop even though the signal looks fine.

Pattern: status OPERATIONAL, signal acceptable, packet loss at or below 1 percent, downlink well above 100 Mbps on 5G.
The site looks healthy. Use the 5G FAQ for handset and indoor steps. Do not invent an outage.

Pattern: status DEGRADED, packet loss above 5 percent, signal weaker than -90 dBm.
Severe loss and marginal signal. Quote the open incident. Expect a field visit. Do not promise same-hour restoration.

Pattern: status OFFLINE, or packet loss 100 percent, throughput 0.
The site is down. Dispatch against the open incident. Do not factory-reset the customer's phone as the fix. 4G LTE and 5G use the same offline rule.

Pattern: status MAINTENANCE and the incident classification is PLANNED_MAINTENANCE.
Quote the window end. Planned maintenance announced at least 48 hours ahead is not an SLA credit by itself.

Pattern: status OPERATIONAL, newest sample healthy, incident status MONITORING.
The site is in service. Say it is being watched. Do not tell the customer it is down.

A regional summary is a count of towers by status in one region. It is not a count of historical outages. Historical questions (how many CRITICAL, which region, how long, how many customers) use the outage log and section 2.

11. Runbooks

POWER
Confirm status OFFLINE or a power alarm. Check the generator. One technician on site for a single tower. If a regional gateway also lost power, classify the outage CRITICAL under section 2 and start the 4-hour MTTR clock. Customer message: the site has no power, here is the incident id, updates follow the cadence in section 6.

BACKHAUL
The tower may stay DEGRADED or even OPERATIONAL while throughput collapses. Fiber cuts on a metro ring are CRITICAL when they isolate a region or affect 5,000 or more customers. A single congested hop affecting under 500 customers is MINOR or MAJOR based on section 2. Customer message: the site can see the phone, but the path behind the site is impaired.

Radio unit, antenna, or scheduler. Intermittent drops with an acceptable signal and rising packet loss belong here. Replace the radio if loss stays above 5 percent across the newest samples. Customer message: the site is on the air and is dropping sessions; a ticket is open.

12. Worked questions

What defines a CRITICAL outage?
Any one of: 5,000 or more customers lost voice or data; a regional core, packet gateway, or metro fiber ring failed; two or more towers in the same city are OFFLINE; or voice and data are fully down and restoration is expected to take more than 60 minutes.

What is the difference between MAJOR and CRITICAL?
MAJOR is 500 to 4,999 customers, or one tower OFFLINE for more than 30 minutes, or impaired service for more than 30 minutes, and none of the CRITICAL rules match. Slow data with calls still completing is not CRITICAL by itself.

Which region had the most CRITICAL outages?
Count rows in the outage log where severity is CRITICAL, grouped by region. Do not count MAJOR and MINOR in that total. Do not answer from this document. The log is the source. A September-only question is a different cut from an all-year question. Filter on the start time before comparing.

This policy is the source of truth for what a Prodapt customer pays to use a phone outside the United States. It defines Zones A through D, Travel Pass daily rates, pay-per-use rates, and the spend cap.

It does not list which towers are up, and it does not list charges already posted to a bill. Posted charges are in the billing system. If a roaming charge looks duplicated, use the billing disputes policy.

Zone A — Canada and Mexico
Countries: Canada, Mexico.

Zone B — Western Europe
Countries: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom.
Western Europe in this policy means Zone B and only the countries in this list. Eastern Europe is not Zone B.

Zone C — selected Asia-Pacific partners
Countries: Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand.
Japan is in Zone C. Japan is not in Zone B and is not charged at Western Europe rates.

Zone D — rest of world
Every other country where Prodapt has a roaming partner. If a country is not listed in Zone A, B, or C, it is Zone D.
Prodapt does not offer satellite roaming, maritime roaming, or in-flight roaming. Those sessions are blocked.

3. Travel Pass daily rates

A Travel Pass covers one line for one calendar day in the customer's local time, from 00:00 through 23:59 in that time zone. A day is billed only if the line registers on a foreign network that day.

- Unlimited calls and texts to the United States.
- Unlimited calls and texts to numbers in the country where the customer is roaming.
- Calls to other countries are pay-per-use at the Zone D voice rate.

A Travel Pass does not include tethering beyond the high-speed allotment, and it does not include international calls placed from the United States to another country. Those are a separate international long-distance rate of 0.15 USD per minute.

Unlimited Plus includes Zone A. A customer on Unlimited Plus pays 0.00 USD for Zone A roaming. They do not need a Zone A Travel Pass. Zone B, Zone C, and Zone D are not included on Unlimited Plus.

1. Purpose

This policy states the uptime targets Prodapt publishes, the mean time to restore (MTTR) targets Network Operations works to, and the rules that decide whether a customer receives an automatic service credit after an outage.

Live outage facts (which region, how long, how many customers, what root cause) are not in this document. Those facts are in the network outage log. A credit decision needs both: the outage facts from the log, and the eligibility rules in this policy.

2. Monthly uptime targets

These targets are reporting goals for a calendar month. They do not, by themselves, create a bill credit. Automatic credits are decided only by the continuous-outage table in section 4.

Account type     Monthly uptime target     What the target means
Consumer         99.5 percent              About 3 hours 39 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month
Business         99.9 percent              About 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month
Enterprise       99.99 percent             About 4 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month

Uptime is measured on the Prodapt radio access and core network for the customer's service region. It does not include the customer's handset, Wi-Fi router, inside wiring, or a third-party network while roaming.

3. MTTR targets

Severity     Restore target     Customer update cadence while the event is open
CRITICAL     4 hours            Every 30 minutes
MAJOR        8 hours            Every 60 minutes
MINOR        24 hours           Every 4 hours

MTTR is the time from the outage start to restoration of voice and data for the affected region or site. Missing an MTTR target is an operations issue. It does not change the credit thresholds in section 4. A CRITICAL event that is restored in 3 hours has met MTTR and still might not qualify a Consumer for a credit, because the Consumer threshold is 8 hours.

4. Automatic SLA credit eligibility

A customer receives an automatic service credit only when all of the following are true:

a. The event is a Prodapt-owned network outage. Customer equipment, a dead handset battery, Wi-Fi, and indoor coverage gaps are not outages under this policy.

b. The outage is unplanned. Planned maintenance that was announced at least 48 hours in advance does not qualify, even if the maintenance lasts longer than the thresholds below. If a planned window overruns and the overrun itself is logged as an unplanned outage, only the overrun time counts.

c. The customer's service address is in the affected region recorded on the outage.

d. The continuous duration of the outage is at least the minimum for the customer's account type:

Account type     Minimum continuous outage for an automatic SLA credit
Consumer         8 hours
Business         4 hours
Enterprise       2 hours

These are hard thresholds. Prodapt does not round a shorter outage up to the next threshold.

Worked example for a 6 hour outage:

A continuous outage lasts 6 hours.
- A Business account qualifies, because 6 hours is at least 4 hours.
- An Enterprise account qualifies, because 6 hours is at least 2 hours.
- A Consumer account does not qualify for an automatic SLA credit, because 6 hours is below the 8 hour Consumer threshold.

A Consumer on a 6 hour outage may ask for a goodwill review. Goodwill is not guaranteed, is not an SLA credit, and follows the billing dispute policy (including the 50.00 USD auto-approval limit) if any credit is offered.

If the person asking does not give an account type, the correct answer is the table above. Do not assume Consumer. Do not promise a credit until the account type and the service region are known.

5. What "continuous" means

The duration is one uninterrupted loss of service.

- A restoration of less than 5 minutes that fails again does not reset the clock. The intervals are added together.
- A restoration of 5 minutes or more starts a new interval. Only an interval that itself meets the threshold qualifies.
- Degraded but usable service (calls complete, data is slow) is not a total loss and does not start the SLA clock.

Credit in USD = (outage hours / 24) x the customer's monthly recurring charge.

Round to the nearest cent.
The minimum automatic credit is 5.00 USD.
The maximum automatic credit is one full month of monthly recurring charge.
Taxes are not refunded as a separate line. The credit is calculated on the pre-tax monthly recurring charge only.
The credit is applied to the account balance. It is not paid out as cash.

- The failure is inside the customer's premises (handset, battery, SIM seated incorrectly, Wi-Fi, third-party router).
- The account was suspended for non-payment during the outage window.
- The customer already received a goodwill or SLA credit for the same outage and the same line.
